newsitem.title: UK: UK markets to shrug off growing political turmoil.
newsitem.headline: UK markets to shrug off growing political turmoil.

text.p: British financial markets are never pleased to see the ruling Conservative Party in open conflict but as the prospect of a Labour government holds fewer terrors than it once did, analysts do not expect a market meltdown.
John Major's Conservative government endured a tough week last week, losing its parliamentary majority while the split over Europe, a running sore for the Tories, widened further.

Teresa Gorman, a noted Conservative Eurosceptic, poured more fuel on the fire on Monday, announcing she will table a motion in parliament next month demanding a referendum on Britain's European Union membership.
The announcement came just one day after Prime Minister Major went on BBC Television to plead for party unity, suggesting right-wing Eurosceptics will offer him little let-up.
But UK markets were largely unruffled. The December gilt future was 18/32 higher at 110-04 by 1300 GMT, boosted by benign producer price figures and the pound was steady at 2.4570 marks.

The FTSE index of 100 leading British shares was nearly 30 points higher at 3,992.4. "The market is neither spooked by the prospect of a Labour or Conservative government now," said Ciaran Barr, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "It's the uncertainty that hurts."
Elections are due by May 1997 but the government, without a majority, could be forced to go to the polls earlier.
"The only problem is week after week of the Conservative Party ripping itself to shreds," Barr said. "But turkeys don't vote for Christmas and sooner or later most will rally round."
Barr said the spread between 10-year gilts and German Bunds, now at 195 basis points, would be unlikely to gape much more.
"I can't see the spread widening much further. It's not like 1992 when the markets were terrified of a Labour government."

Britain's financial markets took a pounding last week, but that was more due to UK authorities talking down the pound and U.S. Federal Reserve Governor Alan Greenspan hinting that stock markets around the globe are overvalued.
"The pound's fall last week was not down to politics, it was good old profit-taking coupled with the government and Bank of England talking the market down," Barr said.

Sterling fell off a cliff on Tuesday, dropping about nine pfennigs against the mark. But that has to be put in context of a rally of about 12 percent in the past few months. News of political infighting in the government ranks is nothing new.
"It's been amazingly obvious for some time that politics is a mess," John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International told Reuters Financial Television.
"The market assumption is that the government will lose (in May) but that's been the working assumption for some time."
So, the events of the last few days have done little to change the broader view of the markets. But even if they remain unfazed, there is unlikely to be much let-up for the government.
Parliament will debate the political minefield of European policy on Wednesday and Thursday. And the Conservatives look certain to lose another parliamentary seat in a by-election on Thursday.

If that was not enough, on Friday and Saturday, Major and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke will attend a European Union summit in Dublin at which any differences between them could be exposed.

Clarke is adamant Britain must keep its options open on whether or not to join a single European currency. Last Friday, Major pledged his full support for the pro-European Chancellor. But such assurances are seen by some as evidence that there must be some truth to reports about divisions between them.

But it is the way of the financial markets that a week that boasts a monthly monetary meeting between Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George and November retail price figures, will see politics relegated to the backburner again.
And that ignores key U.S. inflation figures. "In truth, the main figures will be out of the U.S. next week," said Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at the Cooperative Bank.
"Gilts remain relatively weak but if Bunds and T-bonds go higher, they will be dragged up."
